title: Ballistic transport in nanodevices based on single-crystalline Cu thin films

paper_content.abstract:
In ballistic transport, the movement of charged carriers remains unimpeded by scattering
events. In this limit, microscopic parameters such as crystal momentum, spin and quantum
phase are well conserved, allowing electrons to maintain their quantum coherence over
longer distances. Nanoscale materials, such as carbon nanotubes, graphene, and nanowires,
can exhibit ballistic transport. However, their scalability in devices is significantly limited.
While deposited metal films offer scalability for nanodevices, their short electronic mean free
paths hinder ballistic transport. In this study, we investigated the electronic transport in
cross-geometry devices fabricated with 90-nm-thick Cu films without grain boundaries. We
demonstrated ballistic transport in devices with channel widths of 150 nm at temperatures
below 85 K via negative bend resistance measurements. Our findings establish a scalable
platform for exploring the intrinsic quantum mechanical properties of Cu, advancing both
the fundamental understanding of quantum transport in metals and its practical
applications in next-generation electronic quantum technologies.
paper_content.introduction:
When the electronic mean free path exceeds the device size, electrons undergo ballistic transport
within the device, experiencing minimal scattering. Ballistic transport can reveal intrinsic
quantum properties of solid-state materials, as electrons' quantum information—such as crystal
momentum, spin, and quantum phase—is well conserved1-4. Research on quantum properties of
normal metals, including electronic band structure, Fermi surface topology, conductivity, and
magnetoresistance has accelerated in recent years5-12. Cu is used in electronic circuits owing to
its conductivity, reliability, and versatility. It remains crucial in the electronics industry, used for
high-speed data-processing cables and interconnects in advanced semiconductor devices.
Electronic band structure, Fermi surface topology and Fermi velocity of bulk Cu are well
understood through various measurements13-19. However, growing atomically flat and uniform
Cu thin films without grain boundaries has been technically challenging, and in-plane ballistic
transport in Cu thin film nanostructures has not been achieved, limiting the exploitation of their
intrinsic quantum properties. Although polycrystalline Cu thin films prepared by sputtering and
post-annealing have shown low room-temperature resistivities20 (2.0–2.2×10-8 Ω·m), ballistic
transport was not explicitly examined.

In this study, we demonstrated ballistic transport in nanoscale devices composed of atomically
flat single-crystalline Cu(111) thin films (SCCFs) (Supplementary Fig. 1) grown using the atomic
sputtering epitaxy (ASE) technique21. This method addresses challenges in conventional metal-
film deposition, such as surface oxidation and electrical performance degradation due to defects
such as GBs and impurities22. We observed negative bend resistance in cross-geometry devices,
indicating ballistic transport23. The electronic mean free path of the 80-nm-thick SCCF was 150
nm at a temperature below 85 K (Supplementary Fig. 2). Our SCCF enables studies on the quantum
nature of Cu thin films, including topological properties24-26 and phase-coherent quantum
interference27,28. It also suggests potential applications in quantum circuits, spintronic devices, and
Cu interconnect technology29-31.

Structural defects in the SCCF and a polycrystalline Cu thin film (PCCF)

We analyzed the crystallographic microstructure of the SCCF, as high crystalline quality is
essential for ballistic transport. During thin-film growth, GBs and twin boundaries (TBs) form
owing to lattice mismatch with the substrate. While TBs are unavoidable, the formation of GBs
can be suppressed using a growth technique that considers extended atomic distance mismatch
(EADM)22. The distribution of GBs and TBs was analyzed for a polycrystalline Cu thin film
(PCCF; Figs. 2a–c), an SCCF with minimal GBs (Figs. 2d–f), and an SCCF without GBs (Figs.
2g–i) using misorientation line mapping, electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), and SEM43,44.
GBs and TBs are denoted by blue and red lines, respectively, in Fig. 2. PCCF usually contains
both GBs and TBs (enlarged misorientation maps of the boxed areas in a, d, and g left panels are
shown in the right upper panels and those of the boxed areas in the upper panels are shown in the
right lower panels). As shown in Fig. 2a, the PCCF has many grains (a conventional PCCF is
expected to have trillions of grains on the two-inch wafer42 and each grain has a different
orientation, as illustrated by the numbered indicators in the right lower panel of Fig. 2a). The Cu
thin films grown by ASE show perfect alignment along the (111) plane (Fig. 2e) despite the
presence of some GBs (Fig. 2d). The GBs observed in the misorientation line map in Fig. 2d are
close to the TBs; thus, they do not appear as different grains in the EBSD map, as they deviate
slightly from the ideal TB condition of 60° (deviation of 1°–2°)45. These GBs can influence
electronic transport, and thus, we used only the SCCF without GBs in this study. A well-grown
SCCF (Fig. 2g) is devoid of GBs, contains only TBs, and exhibits two orientations I and II (Fig.
2i right lower panel). The crystallographic orientation of the SCCF follows either ABC… or ACB...
stacking, satisfying symmetry operation by 60° rotation (Supplementary Fig. 12). Although the
TB density fluctuates across areas, it remains within the same order of magnitude. Unlike GBs,
TBs minimally affect electrical resistivity because: 1) charged defects do not form around TBs,
resulting in negligible potential variation near TB46,47, and 2) well-matched Fermi surfaces of
adjacent grains on either side of a TB reduce electron wave scattering, as the Fermi surface of Cu
remains unchanged with 60° rotation about the (111) axis33,45,47-49.

antisymmetrized Hall resistivity 𝜌as for different W at 1.7 K as shown in Fig. 4c (see
xy
Supplementary Fig. 14 for 𝜌as measured at 120 K). The observed nonlinear Hall effect at devices
xy
with W = 10 and 1 µm agrees with the results of a recent study45, which revealed the co-existence
of holes and electrons in <205-nm-thick SCCFs without GBs. However, when the width is reduced
to ≤250 nm, the Hall effect becomes linear, which suggests that electrons become the major charge
carriers. To explain this phenomenon in 1D, we calculated and compared effective band structures
of a 2D Cu(111) thin film (Fig. 4d) along specific k-points with those of a 1D Cu(111) rod (Fig.
4e). In the 2D thin-film band structure, both electron and hole orbits are distinctly visible. In
contrast, the 1D structure's band structure appears more complex due to confined geometry in both
out-of-plane and in-plane directions.

The Fermi surface of the 2D thin film shows splitting of degenerate bands due to confined
geometry along the [111] direction (Fig. 4d, left panel). In the periodic zone scheme representation
(Fig. 4d, right panel), the spectral weight of hole bands is prominent45. The 1D structure's Fermi
surface is featureless, offering negligible insights. Thus, we calculated the effective Fermi surface
via band unfolding to 2D (Fig. 4e, left panel). In the unfolded periodic zone scheme (Fig. 4e, right
panel), the spectral density of hole bands is reduced, disconnecting the hole orbits and allowing
electron orbits to dominate. Although the calculation system size is smaller than the actual device,
it shows the trend of reduced hole orbits as geometry approaches 1D. This explains the
experimental observation that the two-carrier model-induced nonlinear Hall effect becomes linear
with decreasing W. For reference, Supplementary Fig. 15 compares the 3D, 2D, and 1D Fermi
surfaces at a given 𝑘 .
𝑧

In this study, we observed ballistic electronic transport in nanodevices based on Cu(111) thin
films and investigated its dependence on film quality. Hall-bar shaped devices were fabricated
with atomically flat 90-nm-thick SCCFs. We obtained negative bend resistance as direct evidence
of ballistic transport. In a perpendicular magnetic field, ballistic electrons are disturbed, increasing
bend resistance. We determined the distributions of GBs and TBs through EBSD measurement
and showed that the Cu thin-film device’s resistivity primarily depended on GBs, remaining
insensitive to TBs. Our experimental observations and theoretical calculations reveal that as the
Cu(111) thin film transitions from 2D to the 1D limit, hole orbits observed in 2D disappear because
of quantum confinement in both out-of-plane and in-plane directions, suggesting transition from
nonlinear Hall effect, driven by two carriers, to a linear Hall effect.

This paper presents a platform for investigating the intrinsic quantum mechanical properties of
Cu, with the potential to advance high-performance electronic55 and spintronic devices through
preservation of quantum information, including momentum, quantum phase, and spin. This
approach may help address critical reliability challenges in semiconductor technology, such as
Joule heating30 and electromigration31 in Cu interconnects29. Recent discoveries reveal that the
Fermi surface of Cu exhibits a topologically nontrivial genus24, opening the door to various
topology-related experiments in ballistic metals24-26.
paper_content.methods:
Preparation of thin SCCFs using the ASE technique

The ASE method involves stacking atoms individually without forming clusters, which can
cause arbitrary deposition. To achieve this, we modified the conventional sputtering system. The
network of conducting wires, including cables, in the conventional sputtering system was upgraded
with single-crystalline Cu wires, fabricated by cutting single crystal Cu wafers in a spiral fashion
using wire electrical discharge machining (EDM). The wafers were sliced from a single-crystal
ingot grown by the Czochralski method. To minimize vibration from ambient noise, we
implemented a mechanical noise reduction system. While such vibrations may not significantly
affect conventional thin film growth, especially for PCCFs, they can cause irreversible stacking
faults that disrupt the initial nucleation and lateral growth processes, particularly the coherent
coplanar merging of nuclei. The thin film growth system creates a stable environment for single-
atom deposition, aiming to achieve atomically flat surfaces through precise stacking of single
atoms.

The optimized sputtering conditions were as follows:
• Substrate: A double-sided polished (001) Al 2 O 3 wafer with a thickness of 430 μm.
• Deposition temperature: Approximately 170 °C.
• RF power: 13.56 MHz at 30 W.
• Target-to-substrate distance: 95 mm.
• Base pressure: Maintained at less than 2 × 10−7 Torr.
• Working pressure: 5.4 × 10−3 Torr with an Ar gas (99.9999% (6N)) flow of 50 sccm.
The relationship between the deposition time and thickness of the thin film (or the average growth
rate) was determined from the average deposition time of a 200-nm-thick film grown under
optimal conditions.

Sample nanofabrication and transport measurement

To fabricate Hall bar devices using the prepared SCCFs, we partially removed sections of single-
crystalline Cu via electron beam lithography and Ar-ion milling, forming Hall bars with varying
linewidths (Supplementary Fig. 3). After the Ar-ion milling, Cu redeposition was observed along
the lithography resist sidewalls (Supplementary Fig. 16), but such regions may have only limited
contribution to conduction because they likely exhibit reduced crystallinity. The Cu atomic spacing
was 2.07 Å along the (111) direction, confirming that the pristine crystalline quality of the SCCF
was maintained even after patterning (Fig. 1b). Temperature dependence of the bend resistance
and magnetic field dependence of the Hall resistivity of the SCCF Hall bar devices were measured
in Oxford Instrument Teslatron PT with a base temperature of 1.7 K connected with low-pass RC
filters. GB dependence of bend resistance, magnetic field dependence of bend resistance and
longitudinal resistance of SCCF Hall bar devices were measured in Oxford Instrument Heliox with
a base temperature of 4.3 K connected with low-pass RC filters. Bend and longitudinal resistance
were measured by the DC IV-sweep method by measuring the voltage drop with a Keithley 2000
voltmeter, and the current was applied to 200 nA through Yokogawa GS610 source measure unit
with a load resistance of 100 kΩ. Hall resistance was measured with Delta measurement method
by measuring the voltage drop with low-noise Keithley 2182 nanovoltmeter, and current with 1
mA was applied through low-noise Keithley 6221 current source.

Structural information of Hall bar pattern

To investigate the cross-sectional structure of ballistic transport in the SCCF, the annular dark-
field (ADF) imaging mode of aberration-corrected scanning transmission electron microscopy
(STEM; JEM-ARM200CF, JEOL) at 300 kV was employed. The angle range of the ADF detector
was set to 45–175 mrad, and the semiconvergence angle of the condenser lens was ≈24 mrad. In
combination with STEM imaging, elemental mapping of the Cu films was performed in the same
STEM image mode using electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS; Quantum ER965, Gatan).
Cross-sectional TEM sampling was conducted using the Ga-ion milling and slicing method in a
focused-ion-beam scanning electron microscope (SEM; Helios NanoLab 450, Thermo Fisher
Scientific). Low-energy Ar-ion beam milling at 700 V for 10 min was sequentially performed as a
post-surface treatment to remove the damaged surface layer that usually forms during heavy Ga-
ion beam milling.

Theoretical calculations

The total energy and electronic band structure calculations were performed using the first-
principles density functional theory56 as implemented by Kresse and Joubert57 using the projector
augmented-wave method58. The exchange‒correlation functional was modeled using the
generalized gradient approximation in the Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof form59. All the calculations
were spin-polarized, and the positions of the atoms, as well as the size and shape of the unit cell,
were fully relaxed to obtain the optimized lattice structure. All the atoms of bulk Cu were fully
relaxed until the force on the atom was less than 0.001 eV/Å, and the change in total energy was
less than 10-6 eV. The electron wavefunctions were expanded using a plane-wave basis set with a
cut-off energy of 400 eV for the bulk, slab, and rod calculations. A 12-ML (ML: monolayer)
Cu(111) slab structure was used to simulate the 2D-limit thin film, and a 6-ML×6-ML rod
structure was used for the 1D-limit nanorod. The choice of a 12-ML Cu(111) slab is supported by
thickness-convergence tests on 6-, 9-, and 12-ML slabs (Supplementary Fig. 17). We maintained
a 20-Å-thick vacuum layer to prevent interactions between the periodic images.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
• What are the noteworthy results?
The authors report the growth of high-quality Copper thin films (characterized via TEM and detailed electron backscatter
diffraction (EBSD) maps) on which electron transport measurements, especially bend resistance and Hall resistivity, support
the presence of ballistic transport over length scales of the order of 100 nm.
• Will the work be of significance to the field and related fields? How does it compare to the established literature? If the work
is not original, please provide relevant references.
If the authors can convincingly make the case that their transport data is conclusive and firmly confirm ballistic electron
transport in their Cu thin films, it would be quite a significant achievement. Ballistic copper thin films can have applications in
existing integrated circuit technologies and can find future application in quantum circuits.
The growth methods and related characterization methods of very similar Cu films were previously published by some of the
same authors (see Ref. 18, Kim. S. J., Nature 603, 434 (2022)). What is new here is that these films and their detailed
characterization is combined with detailed charge transport measurements. Some of the authors have extensive experience
with such measurements (e.g. H. -W. Jeong et al., Nano Lett. 2024, 24, 15950 (2024)). To the best of my knowledge there is
no previous work with this detailed connection between Cu thin film morphology and charge transport measurements (at
various temperatures) showing evidence for ballistic transport over such a long length scale (> 100 nm).
• Does the work support the conclusions and claims, or is additional evidence needed?
To the best of my assessment, the work partially supports the claims, and I suggest additional data and/or clarifications
which would strengthen the claims. In the next sections I also suggest some clarifications regarding the data analysis.
(1) I would respectfully request that you please state clearly in the main manuscript the number of devices which were
studied for each set of measurements. Please be specific, how many W=150 nm devices were fabricated? How many of
these were characterized using EBSD? And using charge transport? (do the same for all W’s reported). Most importantly:
please clearly state if the EBSD data reported in Figs. 2 and 3 are from the same device as transport data in Figs. 3 and 4?
The strength of the argument is modified significantly if the data are from different devices or the same devices. If the data
are from the same devices, please identify clearly which data points in Fig. 3 and 4 correspond to the Grain Boundary (GB)
maps in Figs. 2 and 3.
(2) Please give more information, and show more raw data in the supplemental information, about the charge transport
measurements. Specifically, please show how the bend resistance, RB, is modified when you use various set of contact
terminals for the current injection and VB measurements. Show the results for all contact configurations in the supplemental
information, for each device showing ballistic transport.
(3) While I found the discussion of Figure 4 interesting, the data reported only marginally supports the discussion. Indeed,
the expected non-linearity (bump) in RB is not visible in Fig. 4b, and its presence in rho_xy in Fig. 4e is speculative at best.
Moreover, there is no discussion of the magnetic field value Bo at which you expect the cyclotron orbit radius to match the
width of the Hall bar (expected B-field location of the non-linearity). The experimental data in this section does not support
well the discussion. The discussion and/or data (how many samples have been measured? Do we have the EBSD data for
these?) should be modified to better support each other, or the Figure should be redesigned. I also mention that the cartoon
of the Hall bar used in Fig. 4 does not match well the actual aspect ratio of the W=150 and 250 nm devices which are at the
center of the discussion. Personally, I find that the data in Fig 4b is more interesting and convincing than the one in Fig. 4e,
so I would suggest to perhaps recenter the discussion on this.
• Are there any flaws in the data analysis, interpretation and conclusions? Do these prohibit publication or require revision?
The bend resistance and Hall resistivity measurements are very likely to be sensitive to the choice of contacts in the
narrowest Hall bars because of edge confinement and the asymmetric shape of the devices. Given the very rough electron-
beam lithography for the narrowest Hall bars (poor homogeneity of the thickness and width), it is essential to convince the
reader that the measurements all agree and point to a single conclusion.
Additionally, the data analysis of transport data is based on the van der Pauw method. This method works in the limit of
“point-like” contacts on the outer edge of the sample. Here the contacts are sometimes even larger than the device itself.
It should be clarified what are the error bars (systematic) stemming from using the van der Pauw method in these devices (the
error bars should be larger in the narrower devices from several reasons including the non-uniform thickness).
In my opinion, the main evidence for the ballistic transport data claim is in Fig. 3b and supplementary Fig. 6a. However, the
signal to noise ratio for the claim is close 1, meaning that the scatter of the data point in these two Figures is comparable to
the magnitude of the negative bend resistance. If this could be strengthened by addressing the above (showing if the RB
data are from multiple contact configurations and from devices whose EBSD maps are reported), then I think that the
conclusion could be stronger.
I do command the authors for this work. This is an incredibly complex set of sample preparation and challenging transport
measurements (given the very low resistivity of copper – which gives little signal to noise in transport). This is unique work. I
could be convinced of the validity of their claim, but I would need more evidence that the negative bend resistance is
reproducible and quantitative accurate – and in multiple devices.
• Is the methodology sound? Does the work meet the expected standards in your field?
Yes, the authors are accomplished and barring the above comments, the work is of very high quality.
• Is there enough detail provided in the methods for the work to be reproduced?
Yes, except for the points mentioned above.
References
I found that unfortunately the bibliography is inadequate. Here are a few things which could improve it in my view.
(i) In the introduction, please add several recent references showing the ongoing development in the field. For example, on
line 55 the authors say “in recent years 5-9” but Refs. 5-9 are not recent at all.
(ii) In multiple places no references are given for items which clearly demand one. For example, on line 71 when listing key
ideas to be explored in ballistic copper films, topics such as “the quantum Hall effect”, “quantum confinement”, and “phase-
coherent interference” are all mentioned without any reference. I also would ask that you please delete the mention of
“hydrodynamic electron transport22”. This is a strange point the make because this hydrodynamic regime is reported in
graphene which has vastly different electron-electron and electron-phonon scattering lengths than copper, there is no reason
(except if you discuss it) to expect any hydrodynamic regime in your devices.
(iii) Several more (and recent) references related to the transport measurements would be appreciated. There are other ways
to assess if a device is ballistic (e.g. quantum interferences, or conductance quantization), but none of this is mentioned.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The paper discusses ballistic electron transport in 90-nm-thick films made of high-quality Cu. The copper films are grown
using the atomic sputtering epitaxy technique, which allows obtaining a very large grain structure with atomically smooth
interfaces. An extensive analysis has been performed to confirm grain boundary-free regions on the Cu films over micron-
sized areas. Transport measurements in the magnetic field of a cross geometry of different sizes support the claim of the
ballistic propagation of electrons at low temperatures.
The reported results raise several issues, which raise concerns about the validity of the results and analysis. These issues
are mainly relevant to transport measurements, but not limited to them. Below, I give a list of the problems that I have found.
1. The paper does not seem to discuss the available literature on the current state of the problem. At least one paper claims
that polycrystalline Cu at room temperature shows better resistivity than that reported in the manuscript. [1]
2. SFig. 4 shows a 250 nm wide sample. However, I do not understand how the sizes were calculated, as I tried to
demonstrate in the image below. It is also unclear what the origin of the Cu regions, highlighted in yellow ellipses in (c), is. If
it were a standard lithography and lift-off process, I would say these are left over after a lift-off process. The Methods have not
provided details on the fabrication method besides lines 397-399. The SEM image in SFig. 3 is blurred, as is evident from a
poorly focused image, as seen by a substantial difference (presence and absence of small features) on SFig. 3a and SFig.
3b. I could say that the size determined by SEM is incorrect, as HAADF-STEM achieved subatomic resolution and should be
more accurate. Anyway, the image also shows that the profile of the device is not a simple rectangle; moreover, it has
parasitic parallel (presumably conducting) channels due to Cu left-overs.
3. Fig.1d shows bend resistance as a function of temperature. I think the experimental results are too close to zero
temperature, even for the minimum temperature of T=1.7 K. The behaviour of the 250 nm sample looks very good due to the
agreement between high-temperature resistances. This can be viewed as perfect uniformity of the grown samples; however,
the lower resistance of the narrowest sample is very surprising at high temperatures. This difference is not discussed in the
text. The line that separates diffusing and ballistic transport regimes is misleading, as some electrons can propagate
ballistically even in a diffusive regime. When a significant part of the electrons are ballistic, the bend resistance should
deviate from the expected behaviour obtained from the theory for the wide samples. the 250 nm wide sample demonstrates a
clear ballistic transport as it differs from the theory.
4. αel-ph should have units. The Debye temperature obtained from the fit, 270K, differs from that found in the literature,
ѲR=330K. This can be related to the thickness or grain boundaries or something else. There is no discussion on the topic.
The Bloch–Gruneisen formula for (line 103) has a missing power of 5 in the T/ѲR prefactor. Maybe this is why I could not
reproduce the fitting parameters reported. My graph below is given for the αel-ph=7e-6 Ωcm and ѲR=270K. The Python
code is provided.
5. The authors should provide the parameters they used for calculating the mean free path in formula (2), including the
effective mass of the electrons in copper, the Fermi velocity, and how they calculated the concentration.
6. Fig. 4b has different bend resistances at zero magnetic field compared with Fig. 1d. Does the system become more
ballistic between the measurements? It would be good if there were more than one sample using a standard van der Pauw
(with 90 degrees rotation and inversion of the magnetic field), as the authors used DC, which is sensitive to any DC bias due
to the Seebeck effect. The ballistic transport complicated it due to the high sensitivity of scattering from the edges. Thus, it is
helpful to show that the negative bend resistance is observed in all realisations of the van der Pauw method [2].
7. The quantum size effect arises when the film's thickness is comparable to the de Broglie wavelength of the electrons in
copper. Thus, this effect is highly unlikely to influence the Hall effect [3]. The thickness of 90 nm corresponds to >400 unit
cells. Independent of the quantization, the high current used in the measurements, 1mA, suggests testing the heating effects
at low temperatures. Also, the profile of the copper conductor is not rectangular, as can be seen in SFig. 4c, and obviously,
this asymmetry is more substantial for narrower samples. There is no such problem in 2D samples, but for 3D wires, the Hall
voltage is not the same on the side walls and can generate a classical magnetoresistance in a perpendicular magnetic field.
8. The main problem of the reported results is massive degradation of mobility (by a factor of 50) in copper compared to
polycrystal bulk copper, as demonstrated in SFig. 2. Thus, it is unclear why this result could be reported as a novelty. I do
not see any simple correlation between the absence of GB and “high” quality of such samples. Probably it is related to scattering
on the edges. In the paper [1], the resistivity of thin films is better at room temperature, which is most relevant to applications.
9. If the primary source of scattering is related to scattering from the edges, then the narrow samples should have a lower
mean free path. This is possible if we compare the mean free path of 170 nm with the reported widths of the devices.
Please note that the samples of 250 nm and 150 nm wide show ballistic transport; however, it is hard to compare where the
ballistic transport is larger. More negative signals do not mean more ballistic transport. More resistive samples with the same
mobility give more negative bend resistance. You can see it directly from the formula (4). Assume r0 = h/4e, PL=PR=PLR << PFW, that means most of the electrons are going forward. Then RB≈-r0/PLR. If PLR is larger (for wider samples, assuming
scattering on the edges), then the negative bend resistance is smaller. In the case PLR=PFW, RB≈0. This means you have
a few scattering events, which means the mean free path is comparable to the size of the sample.
10. Please check the formula (3), as the reference gives a different interpretation and power of -1. There is also a recent
application to gold [4].
References
[1] A. Mallikarjunan, S. Sharma and S. P. Murarka “Resistivity of Copper Films at Thicknesses Near the Mean Free Path of
Electrons in Copper Minimization of the Diffuse Scattering in Copper” Electrochem. Solid-State Lett. 3, 437 (2000)
https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1149/1.1391172/pdf
[2] van der Pauw, L.J. "A method of measuring specific resistivity and Hall effect of discs of arbitrary shape" (PDF). Philips
Research Reports. 13, 1–9 (1958).
https://pearl-hifi.com/06_Lit_Archive/02_PEARL_Arch/Vol_16/Sec_53/Philips_Rsrch_Reports_1946_thru_1977/Philips
Research Reports-13-1958.pdf
[3] G. Govindaraj and V. Devanathan Quantum size effect in thin metal films Phys. Rev. B 34, 5904 (1986).
https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.34.5904
[4] Weigang Ma, Xing Zhang and Koji Takahashi "Electrical properties and reduced Debye temperature of polycrystalline
thin gold films" J. Phys. D: Appl. Phys. 43 (2010).
https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/0022-3727/43/46/465301
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
Referee Report
I have reviewed the manuscript with interest. The authors report on ballistic transport in high-quality copper films and present
a systematic study of the impact of grain boundaries on ballistic conduction. These are timely and relevant findings that
could, in principle, merit publication. However, the presentation and writing currently do not meet the standards expected for
Nature Communications. Below I outline my specific comments.
Major Comments
1. Debye Temperature
The extracted Debye temperature is significantly lower than the commonly reported value for copper (~343 K). The authors
should explain this discrepancy. Is this due to material quality, finite-size effects, or the fitting method used? Clarifying this
point is important to substantiate the validity of the extracted phonon parameters.
2. Estimation of Mean Free Path
Can the authors extract the Hall mobility from their data (e.g., via a multi-band model fit)? If so, they could estimate the
electronic mean free path independently. Such a value would provide a useful consistency check for their claims of ballistic
transport.
3. Reversibility of Bend Resistance Measurements
Have the authors verified the reversibility of their bend resistance experiments—for instance, by reversing current direction
or interchanging current and voltage probes? Without such tests, it is difficult to rule out geometric effects or other
measurement artifacts as the origin of the observed negative bend resistance.
4. Figure Quality
The quality of several figures needs improvement. In particular, font sizes are too small in Fig. 4a and in the tables of Fig. 2c,
f, and i, making them difficult to read. Figures must be legible when printed and should meet the journal’s formatting
standards.
5. References and Justification
Some references appear unrelated to the claims in the main text. For example:
o Line 73: None of the cited papers mention ballistic transport. If these are meant to motivate the use of ballistic copper
interconnects, the rationale must be explicitly stated and supported by appropriate references.
________________________________________
Minor Comments
Main Text:
• L29: We believe that collisions with the sample’s edge cannot be neglected and are most likely still dominating. We
recommend rephrasing the statement.
• L71: The absence of defect-induced scattering alone does not justify the emergence of hydrodynamic transport. In metals,
the high carrier density screens the Coulomb interactions needed for this regime. If the authors believe hydrodynamics might
appear in these SCCF Cu films, they must provide strong motivation and suitable references.
• L79 (Fig. 1a): Please explain what the red dashed line represents.
• L107: A reference should be provided to support the reported electron-phonon coupling values, ideally comparing with
either ab initio or experimental data from the literature.
• L113: Define all symbols clearly. Specify the values used for Fermi velocity and charge carrier density.
• L121: A reference should support the statement made here.
• L194: Clarify whether "ρ_I" refers to the total resistivity, including the grain boundary contribution. If so, consider
reformulating the sentence for precision.
Supplementary Information:
• L33: The term "actual" is vague—please clarify what is meant.
• L43: There appears to be a mismatch in line color between the figure and its legend—this should be corrected.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
We deeply appreciate all the reviewers for reviewing our manuscript and providing valuable
suggestions and advice to strengthen the manuscript. We have revised our manuscript
according to the reviewer’s comments and addressed the issues raised by the reviewers
point-by-point in this response letter. Reviewers’ comments are written in black, authors’
responses are written in blue, and the changes made in the manuscript are written in red.
REVIEWER COMMENTS
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
• What are the noteworthy results?
Reviewer: The authors report the growth of high-quality Copper thin films (characterized
via TEM and detailed electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) maps) on which electron
transport measurements, especially bend resistance and Hall resistivity, support the
presence of ballistic transport over length scales of the order of 100 nm.
• Will the work be of significance to the field and related fields? How does it compare to
the established literature? If the work is not original, please provide relevant references.
Reviewer: If the authors can convincingly make the case that their transport data is
conclusive and firmly confirm ballistic electron transport in their Cu thin films, it would be
quite a significant achievement. Ballistic copper thin films can have applications in existing
integrated circuit technologies and can find future application in quantum circuits.
The growth methods and related characterization methods of very similar Cu films were
previously published by some of the same authors (see Ref. 18, Kim. S. J., Nature 603, 434
(2022)). What is new here is that these films and their detailed characterization is combined
with detailed charge transport measurements. Some of the authors have extensive
experience with such measurements (e.g. H. -W. Jeong et al., Nano Lett. 2024, 24, 15950
(2024)). To the best of my knowledge there is no previous work with this detailed
connection between Cu thin film morphology and charge transport measurements (at
various temperatures) showing evidence for ballistic transport over such a long length
scale (> 100 nm).
Response: We would like to express our sincere gratitude for the reviewer’s insightful
evaluation, valuable comments, and encouraging remarks on this manuscript.
• Does the work support the conclusions and claims, or is additional evidence needed?
Reviewer: To the best of my assessment, the work partially supports the claims, and I
suggest additional data and/or clarifications which would strengthen the claims. In the
next sections I also suggest some clarifications regarding the data analysis.
Response: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s positive evaluation and the suggestions
for potential improvements. We will carefully address all the comments and points
mentioned below to ensure they are fully incorporated.
Reviewer: (1) I would respectfully request that you please state clearly in the main
manuscript the number of devices which were studied for each set of measurements.
Please be specific, how many W=150 nm devices were fabricated? How many of these
were characterized using EBSD? And using charge transport? (do the same for all W’s
reported). Most importantly: please clearly state if the EBSD data reported in Figs. 2 and 3
are from the same device as transport data in Figs. 3 and 4? The strength of the argument
is modified significantly if the data are from different devices or the same devices. If the
data are from the same devices, please identify clearly which data points in Fig. 3 and 4
correspond to the Grain Boundary (GB) maps in Figs. 2 and 3.
Response: Here, W denotes the nominal (designed) channel width, which may differ from
the actual one. In all devices measured, the actual channel width deviated by no more
than ~10 % from the designed width. A total of 25 single-crystalline Cu(111) films were
fabricated into devices for this study. In total, 76 Hall bar devices were prepared: 1 device
with W = 10 μm (for comparison with the 1 μm device in Fig. 1d), 25 devices with W = 1
μm, 25 devices with W = 250 nm, and 25 devices with W = 150 nm. All samples from the
25 films were measured for their electrical transport properties in Fig. 3b, while a few films
out of 25 were measured for their electrical transport properties in Figs. 1 and 4. In our
experimental procedure, the samples were first grown and then characterized by EBSD.
Devices were subsequently fabricated from these EBSD-characterized samples, meaning
that 100% of the samples used for device fabrication were measured by EBSD in advance.
Regarding the reviewer’s question, “Most importantly: please clearly state if the EBSD data
reported in Figs. 2 and 3 are from the same device as transport data in Figs. 3 and 4?”,
each point in Fig. 3b corresponds to a single film, and each device was fabricated either
on a different film or on a different location of the same film. Therefore, the misorientation
line map from EBSD shown in Fig. 3b represents only one example among the samples in
each category, and not all samples in the same category have the same misorientation
map. Nevertheless, the samples classified in the same category have comparable GB
densities and exhibit similar transport behaviour, as described.
More specifically, as the reviewer requested, the three misorientation line maps presented
in the lower panel of Fig. 3b correspond to the representative films located around -9

width of 150 nm and gradually widen toward the wire-bonding regions.
From a theoretical standpoint, the so-called “Greek cross” geometry (Fig. R1-5a) we employ
is one of the most robust configurations for minimizing systematic errors from finite
contact size. As described in the references [R3, R4], the error E can be quantitatively

the contact pad. Given that the contact length is at least 200 nm as shown in Fig. R1-5b,

boundaries (GBs) and the high quality of such samples is not consistent with established

properties depend on the number of grain boundaries (GBs). By eliminating these grain

We thank the reviewer for the comment. However, However, it seems there was some confusion

widths lead to differences in carrier properties due to geometric confinement, as further illustrated

We emphasize that the confined geometry effect discussed here is distinct from the quantum
confinement effect raised by the reviewer. Quantum confinement leads to the formation of
standing waves in a narrow device with the number of modes determined by the ratio of device
size to the Fermi wavelength. In our case, however, geometric confinement modifies carrier
properties without invoking quantum standing-wave effects, and this distinction has been
addressed in our analysis.

• “When the electronic mean free path is longer than the device size, electrons exhibit
ballistic transport without significant scattering from phonons…” Personally, this phrase might be
confusing, as I can choose any size of the device. In this case, it is unclear what can be called
significant, as ballistic transport is a relative quantity, but scattering probability has an absolute

Authors’ Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s comment. In the opening sentence, our intent
was to provide a general, qualitative definition of ballistic transport. We were not implying that
the intrinsic electronic properties of the material change with device size. To clarify this point, we
have revised the following sentence on page 2, lines 48–49 in the main text.
“When the electronic mean free path exceeds the device size, electrons undergo ballistic transport
within the device, experiencing minimal scattering.”
We also clarify that scattering rate during transport within devices can depend on device geometry
such as film thickness and channel width. When the film thickness or channel width is reduced,
surface and sidewall scattering become more prominent and the scattering probability increases.
This dependence on geometry is explicitly described in the Fuchs–Sondheimer model for thin
metallic films [R1] and in studies of metallic nanowires [R2]. In this context, “mean free path” refers
to the transport mean free path extracted from our device-level measurements. The transport
mean free path describes the electron’s behavior in the specific device, where both elastic
scattering and inelastic scattering play a role, while the elastic mean free path characterizes only
elastic events. Since the ‘electron mean free path’ in this work is obtained from transport
measurements, it should be interpreted as a transport mean free path.
• “Ballistic transport reveals intrinsic quantum properties of solid-state materials, as electrons’
quantum information—such as crystal momentum, spin, and quantum phase—is well conserved.”
Transport MFP and spin coherence length are different quantities. Quantum phase is even more
subtle in metals and is related to a phase coherence length. I expect it to be significantly larger
at low temperatures than the smallest 150 nm device you have used [Phys. Rev. B 68, 085413
(2003)].

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

In ballistic transport, the movement of charged carriers remains unimpeded by scattering
events. In this limit, microscopic parameters such as crystal momentum, spin and quantum
phase are well conserved, allowing electrons to maintain their quantum coherence over
longer distances. Nanoscale materials, such as carbon nanotubes, graphene, and nanowires,
can exhibit ballistic transport. However, their scalability in devices is significantly limited.
While deposited metal films offer scalability for nanodevices, their short electronic mean free
paths hinder ballistic transport. In this study, we investigated the electronic transport in
cross-geometry devices fabricated with 90-nm-thick Cu films without grain boundaries. We
demonstrated ballistic transport in devices with channel widths of 150 nm at temperatures
below 85 K via negative bend resistance measurements. Our findings establish a scalable
platform for exploring the intrinsic quantum mechanical properties of Cu, advancing both
the fundamental understanding of quantum transport in metals and its practical
applications in next-generation electronic quantum technologies.

---

## Introduction

When the electronic mean free path exceeds the device size, electrons undergo ballistic transport
within the device, experiencing minimal scattering. Ballistic transport can reveal intrinsic
quantum properties of solid-state materials, as electrons' quantum information—such as crystal
momentum, spin, and quantum phase—is well conserved1-4. Research on quantum properties of
normal metals, including electronic band structure, Fermi surface topology, conductivity, and
magnetoresistance has accelerated in recent years5-12. Cu is used in electronic circuits owing to
its conductivity, reliability, and versatility. It remains crucial in the electronics industry, used for
high-speed data-processing cables and interconnects in advanced semiconductor devices.
Electronic band structure, Fermi surface topology and Fermi velocity of bulk Cu are well
understood through various measurements13-19. However, growing atomically flat and uniform
Cu thin films without grain boundaries has been technically challenging, and in-plane ballistic
transport in Cu thin film nanostructures has not been achieved, limiting the exploitation of their
intrinsic quantum properties. Although polycrystalline Cu thin films prepared by sputtering and
post-annealing have shown low room-temperature resistivities20 (2.0–2.2×10-8 Ω·m), ballistic
transport was not explicitly examined.

In this study, we demonstrated ballistic transport in nanoscale devices composed of atomically
flat single-crystalline Cu(111) thin films (SCCFs) (Supplementary Fig. 1) grown using the atomic
sputtering epitaxy (ASE) technique21. This method addresses challenges in conventional metal-
film deposition, such as surface oxidation and electrical performance degradation due to defects
such as GBs and impurities22. We observed negative bend resistance in cross-geometry devices,
indicating ballistic transport23. The electronic mean free path of the 80-nm-thick SCCF was 150
nm at a temperature below 85 K (Supplementary Fig. 2). Our SCCF enables studies on the quantum
nature of Cu thin films, including topological properties24-26 and phase-coherent quantum
interference27,28. It also suggests potential applications in quantum circuits, spintronic devices, and
Cu interconnect technology29-31.

---

Structural defects in the SCCF and a polycrystalline Cu thin film (PCCF)

We analyzed the crystallographic microstructure of the SCCF, as high crystalline quality is
essential for ballistic transport. During thin-film growth, GBs and twin boundaries (TBs) form

can be suppressed using a growth technique that considers extended atomic distance mismatch
(EADM)22. The distribution of GBs and TBs was analyzed for a polycrystalline Cu thin film

The Fermi surface of the 2D thin film shows splitting of degenerate bands due to confined

(Fig. 4d, right panel), the spectral weight of hole bands is prominent45. The 1D structure's Fermi
surface is featureless, offering negligible insights. Thus, we calculated the effective Fermi surface
via band unfolding to 2D (Fig. 4e, left panel). In the unfolded periodic zone scheme (Fig. 4e, right
panel), the spectral density of hole bands is reduced, disconnecting the hole orbits and allowing
electron orbits to dominate. Although the calculation system size is smaller than the actual device,
it shows the trend of reduced hole orbits as geometry approaches 1D. This explains the
experimental observation that the two-carrier model-induced nonlinear Hall effect becomes linear
with decreasing W. For reference, Supplementary Fig. 15 compares the 3D, 2D, and 1D Fermi

𝑧

In this study, we observed ballistic electronic transport in nanodevices based on Cu(111) thin
films and investigated its dependence on film quality. Hall-bar shaped devices were fabricated
with atomically flat 90-nm-thick SCCFs. We obtained negative bend resistance as direct evidence
of ballistic transport. In a perpendicular magnetic field, ballistic electrons are disturbed, increasing
bend resistance. We determined the distributions of GBs and TBs through EBSD measurement
and showed that the Cu thin-film device’s resistivity primarily depended on GBs, remaining
insensitive to TBs. Our experimental observations and theoretical calculations reveal that as the
Cu(111) thin film transitions from 2D to the 1D limit, hole orbits observed in 2D disappear because
of quantum confinement in both out-of-plane and in-plane directions, suggesting transition from
nonlinear Hall effect, driven by two carriers, to a linear Hall effect.

This paper presents a platform for investigating the intrinsic quantum mechanical properties of
Cu, with the potential to advance high-performance electronic55 and spintronic devices through
preservation of quantum information, including momentum, quantum phase, and spin. This
approach may help address critical reliability challenges in semiconductor technology, such as
Joule heating30 and electromigration31 in Cu interconnects29. Recent discoveries reveal that the
Fermi surface of Cu exhibits a topologically nontrivial genus24, opening the door to various
topology-related experiments in ballistic metals24-26.

---

## Methods

Preparation of thin SCCFs using the ASE technique

The ASE method involves stacking atoms individually without forming clusters, which can
cause arbitrary deposition. To achieve this, we modified the conventional sputtering system. The
network of conducting wires, including cables, in the conventional sputtering system was upgraded
with single-crystalline Cu wires, fabricated by cutting single crystal Cu wafers in a spiral fashion
using wire electrical discharge machining (EDM). The wafers were sliced from a single-crystal
ingot grown by the Czochralski method. To minimize vibration from ambient noise, we
implemented a mechanical noise reduction system. While such vibrations may not significantly
affect conventional thin film growth, especially for PCCFs, they can cause irreversible stacking
faults that disrupt the initial nucleation and lateral growth processes, particularly the coherent
coplanar merging of nuclei. The thin film growth system creates a stable environment for single-
atom deposition, aiming to achieve atomically flat surfaces through precise stacking of single
atoms.

The optimized sputtering conditions were as follows:
• Substrate: A double-sided polished (001) Al 2 O 3 wafer with a thickness of 430 μm.
• Deposition temperature: Approximately 170 °C.
• RF power: 13.56 MHz at 30 W.
• Target-to-substrate distance: 95 mm.
• Base pressure: Maintained at less than 2 × 10−7 Torr.
• Working pressure: 5.4 × 10−3 Torr with an Ar gas (99.9999% (6N)) flow of 50 sccm.
The relationship between the deposition time and thickness of the thin film (or the average growth
rate) was determined from the average deposition time of a 200-nm-thick film grown under
optimal conditions.

Sample nanofabrication and transport measurement

To fabricate Hall bar devices using the prepared SCCFs, we partially removed sections of single-
crystalline Cu via electron beam lithography and Ar-ion milling, forming Hall bars with varying
linewidths (Supplementary Fig. 3). After the Ar-ion milling, Cu redeposition was observed along
the lithography resist sidewalls (Supplementary Fig. 16), but such regions may have only limited
contribution to conduction because they likely exhibit reduced crystallinity. The Cu atomic spacing
was 2.07 Å along the (111) direction, confirming that the pristine crystalline quality of the SCCF
was maintained even after patterning (Fig. 1b). Temperature dependence of the bend resistance
and magnetic field dependence of the Hall resistivity of the SCCF Hall bar devices were measured
in Oxford Instrument Teslatron PT with a base temperature of 1.7 K connected with low-pass RC
filters. GB dependence of bend resistance, magnetic field dependence of bend resistance and
longitudinal resistance of SCCF Hall bar devices were measured in Oxford Instrument Heliox with
a base temperature of 4.3 K connected with low-pass RC filters. Bend and longitudinal resistance
were measured by the DC IV-sweep method by measuring the voltage drop with a Keithley 2000
voltmeter, and the current was applied to 200 nA through Yokogawa GS610 source measure unit
with a load resistance of 100 kΩ. Hall resistance was measured with Delta measurement method
by measuring the voltage drop with low-noise Keithley 2182 nanovoltmeter, and current with 1
mA was applied through low-noise Keithley 6221 current source.

Structural information of Hall bar pattern

To investigate the cross-sectional structure of ballistic transport in the SCCF, the annular dark-
field (ADF) imaging mode of aberration-corrected scanning transmission electron microscopy
(STEM; JEM-ARM200CF, JEOL) at 300 kV was employed. The angle range of the ADF detector
was set to 45–175 mrad, and the semiconvergence angle of the condenser lens was ≈24 mrad. In
combination with STEM imaging, elemental mapping of the Cu films was performed in the same
STEM image mode using electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS; Quantum ER965, Gatan).
Cross-sectional TEM sampling was conducted using the Ga-ion milling and slicing method in a
focused-ion-beam scanning electron microscope (SEM; Helios NanoLab 450, Thermo Fisher
Scientific). Low-energy Ar-ion beam milling at 700 V for 10 min was sequentially performed as a
post-surface treatment to remove the damaged surface layer that usually forms during heavy Ga-
ion beam milling.

Theoretical calculations

The total energy and electronic band structure calculations were performed using the first-
principles density functional theory56 as implemented by Kresse and Joubert57 using the projector
augmented-wave method58. The exchange‒correlation functional was modeled using the
generalized gradient approximation in the Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof form59. All the calculations
were spin-polarized, and the positions of the atoms, as well as the size and shape of the unit cell,
were fully relaxed to obtain the optimized lattice structure. All the atoms of bulk Cu were fully
relaxed until the force on the atom was less than 0.001 eV/Å, and the change in total energy was
less than 10-6 eV. The electron wavefunctions were expanded using a plane-wave basis set with a
cut-off energy of 400 eV for the bulk, slab, and rod calculations. A 12-ML (ML: monolayer)
Cu(111) slab structure was used to simulate the 2D-limit thin film, and a 6-ML×6-ML rod
structure was used for the 1D-limit nanorod. The choice of a 12-ML Cu(111) slab is supported by
thickness-convergence tests on 6-, 9-, and 12-ML slabs (Supplementary Fig. 17). We maintained
a 20-Å-thick vacuum layer to prevent interactions between the periodic images.

### Reviewer 1

• What are the noteworthy results?
The authors report the growth of high-quality Copper thin films (characterized via TEM and detailed electron backscatter
diffraction (EBSD) maps) on which electron transport measurements, especially bend resistance and Hall resistivity, support
the presence of ballistic transport over length scales of the order of 100 nm.
• Will the work be of significance to the field and related fields? How does it compare to the established literature? If the work
is not original, please provide relevant references.
If the authors can convincingly make the case that their transport data is conclusive and firmly confirm ballistic electron
transport in their Cu thin films, it would be quite a significant achievement. Ballistic copper thin films can have applications in
existing integrated circuit technologies and can find future application in quantum circuits.
The growth methods and related characterization methods of very similar Cu films were previously published by some of the
same authors (see Ref. 18, Kim. S. J., Nature 603, 434 (2022)). What is new here is that these films and their detailed
characterization is combined with detailed charge transport measurements. Some of the authors have extensive experience
with such measurements (e.g. H. -W. Jeong et al., Nano Lett. 2024, 24, 15950 (2024)). To the best of my knowledge there is
no previous work with this detailed connection between Cu thin film morphology and charge transport measurements (at
various temperatures) showing evidence for ballistic transport over such a long length scale (> 100 nm).
• Does the work support the conclusions and claims, or is additional evidence needed?
To the best of my assessment, the work partially supports the claims, and I suggest additional data and/or clarifications
which would strengthen the claims. In the next sections I also suggest some clarifications regarding the data analysis.
(1) I would respectfully request that you please state clearly in the main manuscript the number of devices which were
studied for each set of measurements. Please be specific, how many W=150 nm devices were fabricated? How many of
these were characterized using EBSD? And using charge transport? (do the same for all W’s reported). Most importantly:
please clearly state if the EBSD data reported in Figs. 2 and 3 are from the same device as transport data in Figs. 3 and 4?
The strength of the argument is modified significantly if the data are from different devices or the same devices. If the data
are from the same devices, please identify clearly which data points in Fig. 3 and 4 correspond to the Grain Boundary (GB)
maps in Figs. 2 and 3.
(2) Please give more information, and show more raw data in the supplemental information, about the charge transport
measurements. Specifically, please show how the bend resistance, RB, is modified when you use various set of contact
terminals for the current injection and VB measurements. Show the results for all contact configurations in the supplemental
information, for each device showing ballistic transport.
(3) While I found the discussion of Figure 4 interesting, the data reported only marginally supports the discussion. Indeed,
the expected non-linearity (bump) in RB is not visible in Fig. 4b, and its presence in rho_xy in Fig. 4e is speculative at best.
Moreover, there is no discussion of the magnetic field value Bo at which you expect the cyclotron orbit radius to match the
width of the Hall bar (expected B-field location of the non-linearity). The experimental data in this section does not support
well the discussion. The discussion and/or data (how many samples have been measured? Do we have the EBSD data for
these?) should be modified to better support each other, or the Figure should be redesigned. I also mention that the cartoon
of the Hall bar used in Fig. 4 does not match well the actual aspect ratio of the W=150 and 250 nm devices which are at the
center of the discussion. Personally, I find that the data in Fig 4b is more interesting and convincing than the one in Fig. 4e,
so I would suggest to perhaps recenter the discussion on this.
• Are there any flaws in the data analysis, interpretation and conclusions? Do these prohibit publication or require revision?
The bend resistance and Hall resistivity measurements are very likely to be sensitive to the choice of contacts in the
narrowest Hall bars because of edge confinement and the asymmetric shape of the devices. Given the very rough electron-
beam lithography for the narrowest Hall bars (poor homogeneity of the thickness and width), it is essential to convince the
reader that the measurements all agree and point to a single conclusion.
Additionally, the data analysis of transport data is based on the van der Pauw method. This method works in the limit of
“point-like” contacts on the outer edge of the sample. Here the contacts are sometimes even larger than the device itself.
It should be clarified what are the error bars (systematic) stemming from using the van der Pauw method in these devices (the
error bars should be larger in the narrower devices from several reasons including the non-uniform thickness).
In my opinion, the main evidence for the ballistic transport data claim is in Fig. 3b and supplementary Fig. 6a. However, the
signal to noise ratio for the claim is close 1, meaning that the scatter of the data point in these two Figures is comparable to
the magnitude of the negative bend resistance. If this could be strengthened by addressing the above (showing if the RB
data are from multiple contact configurations and from devices whose EBSD maps are reported), then I think that the
conclusion could be stronger.
I do command the authors for this work. This is an incredibly complex set of sample preparation and challenging transport
measurements (given the very low resistivity of copper – which gives little signal to noise in transport). This is unique work. I
could be convinced of the validity of their claim, but I would need more evidence that the negative bend resistance is
reproducible and quantitative accurate – and in multiple devices.
• Is the methodology sound? Does the work meet the expected standards in your field?
Yes, the authors are accomplished and barring the above comments, the work is of very high quality.
• Is there enough detail provided in the methods for the work to be reproduced?
Yes, except for the points mentioned above.
References
I found that unfortunately the bibliography is inadequate. Here are a few things which could improve it in my view.
(i) In the introduction, please add several recent references showing the ongoing development in the field. For example, on
line 55 the authors say “in recent years 5-9” but Refs. 5-9 are not recent at all.
(ii) In multiple places no references are given for items which clearly demand one. For example, on line 71 when listing key
ideas to be explored in ballistic copper films, topics such as “the quantum Hall effect”, “quantum confinement”, and “phase-
coherent interference” are all mentioned without any reference. I also would ask that you please delete the mention of
“hydrodynamic electron transport22”. This is a strange point the make because this hydrodynamic regime is reported in
graphene which has vastly different electron-electron and electron-phonon scattering lengths than copper, there is no reason
(except if you discuss it) to expect any hydrodynamic regime in your devices.
(iii) Several more (and recent) references related to the transport measurements would be appreciated. There are other ways
to assess if a device is ballistic (e.g. quantum interferences, or conductance quantization), but none of this is mentioned.

### Reviewer 3

Referee Report
I have reviewed the manuscript with interest. The authors report on ballistic transport in high-quality copper films and present
a systematic study of the impact of grain boundaries on ballistic conduction. These are timely and relevant findings that
could, in principle, merit publication. However, the presentation and writing currently do not meet the standards expected for
Nature Communications. Below I outline my specific comments.
Major Comments
1. Debye Temperature
The extracted Debye temperature is significantly lower than the commonly reported value for copper (~343 K). The authors
should explain this discrepancy. Is this due to material quality, finite-size effects, or the fitting method used? Clarifying this
point is important to substantiate the validity of the extracted phonon parameters.
2. Estimation of Mean Free Path
Can the authors extract the Hall mobility from their data (e.g., via a multi-band model fit)? If so, they could estimate the
electronic mean free path independently. Such a value would provide a useful consistency check for their claims of ballistic
transport.
3. Reversibility of Bend Resistance Measurements
Have the authors verified the reversibility of their bend resistance experiments—for instance, by reversing current direction
or interchanging current and voltage probes? Without such tests, it is difficult to rule out geometric effects or other
measurement artifacts as the origin of the observed negative bend resistance.
4. Figure Quality
The quality of several figures needs improvement. In particular, font sizes are too small in Fig. 4a and in the tables of Fig. 2c,
f, and i, making them difficult to read. Figures must be legible when printed and should meet the journal’s formatting
standards.
5. References and Justification
Some references appear unrelated to the claims in the main text. For example:
o Line 73: None of the cited papers mention ballistic transport. If these are meant to motivate the use of ballistic copper
interconnects, the rationale must be explicitly stated and supported by appropriate references.
________________________________________
Minor Comments
Main Text:
• L29: We believe that collisions with the sample’s edge cannot be neglected and are most likely still dominating. We
recommend rephrasing the statement.
• L71: The absence of defect-induced scattering alone does not justify the emergence of hydrodynamic transport. In metals,
the high carrier density screens the Coulomb interactions needed for this regime. If the authors believe hydrodynamics might
appear in these SCCF Cu films, they must provide strong motivation and suitable references.
• L79 (Fig. 1a): Please explain what the red dashed line represents.
• L107: A reference should be provided to support the reported electron-phonon coupling values, ideally comparing with
either ab initio or experimental data from the literature.
• L113: Define all symbols clearly. Specify the values used for Fermi velocity and charge carrier density.
• L121: A reference should support the statement made here.
• L194: Clarify whether "ρ_I" refers to the total resistivity, including the grain boundary contribution. If so, consider
reformulating the sentence for precision.
Supplementary Information:
• L33: The term "actual" is vague—please clarify what is meant.
• L43: There appears to be a mismatch in line color between the figure and its legend—this should be corrected.

## Paper

## Abstract

In ballistic transport, the movement of charged carriers remains unimpeded by scattering
events. In this limit, microscopic parameters such as crystal momentum, spin and quantum
phase are well conserved, allowing electrons to maintain their quantum coherence over
longer distances. Nanoscale materials, such as carbon nanotubes, graphene, and nanowires,
can exhibit ballistic transport. However, their scalability in devices is significantly limited.
While deposited metal films offer scalability for nanodevices, their short electronic mean free
paths hinder ballistic transport. In this study, we investigated the electronic transport in
cross-geometry devices fabricated with 90-nm-thick Cu films without grain boundaries. We
demonstrated ballistic transport in devices with channel widths of 150 nm at temperatures
below 85 K via negative bend resistance measurements. Our findings establish a scalable
platform for exploring the intrinsic quantum mechanical properties of Cu, advancing both
the fundamental understanding of quantum transport in metals and its practical
applications in next-generation electronic quantum technologies.

---

## Introduction

When the electronic mean free path exceeds the device size, electrons undergo ballistic transport
within the device, experiencing minimal scattering. Ballistic transport can reveal intrinsic
quantum properties of solid-state materials, as electrons' quantum information—such as crystal
momentum, spin, and quantum phase—is well conserved1-4. Research on quantum properties of
normal metals, including electronic band structure, Fermi surface topology, conductivity, and
magnetoresistance has accelerated in recent years5-12. Cu is used in electronic circuits owing to
its conductivity, reliability, and versatility. It remains crucial in the electronics industry, used for
high-speed data-processing cables and interconnects in advanced semiconductor devices.
Electronic band structure, Fermi surface topology and Fermi velocity of bulk Cu are well
understood through various measurements13-19. However, growing atomically flat and uniform
Cu thin films without grain boundaries has been technically challenging, and in-plane ballistic
transport in Cu thin film nanostructures has not been achieved, limiting the exploitation of their
intrinsic quantum properties. Although polycrystalline Cu thin films prepared by sputtering and
post-annealing have shown low room-temperature resistivities20 (2.0–2.2×10-8 Ω·m), ballistic
transport was not explicitly examined.

In this study, we demonstrated ballistic transport in nanoscale devices composed of atomically
flat single-crystalline Cu(111) thin films (SCCFs) (Supplementary Fig. 1) grown using the atomic
sputtering epitaxy (ASE) technique21. This method addresses challenges in conventional metal-
film deposition, such as surface oxidation and electrical performance degradation due to defects
such as GBs and impurities22. We observed negative bend resistance in cross-geometry devices,
indicating ballistic transport23. The electronic mean free path of the 80-nm-thick SCCF was 150
nm at a temperature below 85 K (Supplementary Fig. 2). Our SCCF enables studies on the quantum
nature of Cu thin films, including topological properties24-26 and phase-coherent quantum
interference27,28. It also suggests potential applications in quantum circuits, spintronic devices, and
Cu interconnect technology29-31.

---

Structural defects in the SCCF and a polycrystalline Cu thin film (PCCF)

We analyzed the crystallographic microstructure of the SCCF, as high crystalline quality is
essential for ballistic transport. During thin-film growth, GBs and twin boundaries (TBs) form
owing to lattice mismatch with the substrate. While TBs are unavoidable, the formation of GBs
can be suppressed using a growth technique that considers extended atomic distance mismatch
(EADM)22. The distribution of GBs and TBs was analyzed for a polycrystalline Cu thin film
(PCCF; Figs. 2a–c), an SCCF with minimal GBs (Figs. 2d–f), and an SCCF without GBs (Figs.
2g–i) using misorientation line mapping, electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), and SEM43,44.
GBs and TBs are denoted by blue and red lines, respectively, in Fig. 2. PCCF usually contains
both GBs and TBs (enlarged misorientation maps of the boxed areas in a, d, and g left panels are
shown in the right upper panels and those of the boxed areas in the upper panels are shown in the
right lower panels). As shown in Fig. 2a, the PCCF has many grains (a conventional PCCF is
expected to have trillions of grains on the two-inch wafer42 and each grain has a different
orientation, as illustrated by the numbered indicators in the right lower panel of Fig. 2a). The Cu
thin films grown by ASE show perfect alignment along the (111) plane (Fig. 2e) despite the
presence of some GBs (Fig. 2d). The GBs observed in the misorientation line map in Fig. 2d are
close to the TBs; thus, they do not appear as different grains in the EBSD map, as they deviate
slightly from the ideal TB condition of 60° (deviation of 1°–2°)45. These GBs can influence
electronic transport, and thus, we used only the SCCF without GBs in this study. A well-grown
SCCF (Fig. 2g) is devoid of GBs, contains only TBs, and exhibits two orientations I and II (Fig.
2i right lower panel). The crystallographic orientation of the SCCF follows either ABC… or ACB...
stacking, satisfying symmetry operation by 60° rotation (Supplementary Fig. 12). Although the
TB density fluctuates across areas, it remains within the same order of magnitude. Unlike GBs,
TBs minimally affect electrical resistivity because: 1) charged defects do not form around TBs,
resulting in negligible potential variation near TB46,47, and 2) well-matched Fermi surfaces of
adjacent grains on either side of a TB reduce electron wave scattering, as the Fermi surface of Cu
remains unchanged with 60° rotation about the (111) axis33,45,47-49.

of a 2D Cu(111) thin film (Fig. 4d) along specific k-points with those of a 1D Cu(111) rod (Fig.

contrast, the 1D structure's band structure appears more complex due to confined geometry in both

The Fermi surface of the 2D thin film shows splitting of degenerate bands due to confined
geometry along the [111] direction (Fig. 4d, left panel). In the periodic zone scheme representation
(Fig. 4d, right panel), the spectral weight of hole bands is prominent45. The 1D structure's Fermi
surface is featureless, offering negligible insights. Thus, we calculated the effective Fermi surface
via band unfolding to 2D (Fig. 4e, left panel). In the unfolded periodic zone scheme (Fig. 4e, right
panel), the spectral density of hole bands is reduced, disconnecting the hole orbits and allowing
electron orbits to dominate. Although the calculation system size is smaller than the actual device,
it shows the trend of reduced hole orbits as geometry approaches 1D. This explains the
experimental observation that the two-carrier model-induced nonlinear Hall effect becomes linear
with decreasing W. For reference, Supplementary Fig. 15 compares the 3D, 2D, and 1D Fermi
surfaces at a given 𝑘 .
𝑧

In this study, we observed ballistic electronic transport in nanodevices based on Cu(111) thin
films and investigated its dependence on film quality. Hall-bar shaped devices were fabricated
with atomically flat 90-nm-thick SCCFs. We obtained negative bend resistance as direct evidence
of ballistic transport. In a perpendicular magnetic field, ballistic electrons are disturbed, increasing
bend resistance. We determined the distributions of GBs and TBs through EBSD measurement
and showed that the Cu thin-film device’s resistivity primarily depended on GBs, remaining
insensitive to TBs. Our experimental observations and theoretical calculations reveal that as the
Cu(111) thin film transitions from 2D to the 1D limit, hole orbits observed in 2D disappear because
of quantum confinement in both out-of-plane and in-plane directions, suggesting transition from
nonlinear Hall effect, driven by two carriers, to a linear Hall effect.

This paper presents a platform for investigating the intrinsic quantum mechanical properties of
Cu, with the potential to advance high-performance electronic55 and spintronic devices through
preservation of quantum information, including momentum, quantum phase, and spin. This
approach may help address critical reliability challenges in semiconductor technology, such as
Joule heating30 and electromigration31 in Cu interconnects29. Recent discoveries reveal that the
Fermi surface of Cu exhibits a topologically nontrivial genus24, opening the door to various
topology-related experiments in ballistic metals24-26.
